History would suggest that as soon as US ISM business confidence and industrial production growth start to recover, it will unleash powerful forces allowing industrial metal prices to out-perform gold. - **However, we believe commodity markets and specifically crude oil and copper are in danger of overplaying the reflation scenario.** In copper we believe this reflects the market confusing Chinese strategic reserve buying with actual consumer demand. As we stated at the beginning of the year, we believe commodity prices will be prone to false rallies during the first half of this year given the slow nature of the economic upturn. **Figure 1: Awaiting a lower volatility environment ahead** ahead

### **Trade #1: Sell Rallies In Dry Freight** 

We recommend selling any rallies in dry freight.  We find that the most important driver of dry freight rates is the performance of Asian export growth.  Moreover we find that US ISM business confidence index is a six month leading indicator of Asian export growth. 

This would imply that the time to adopt bullish recommendations on dry freight rates would be six months after the US ISM index has strated to turn convincingly higher.  Since we expect the US recession to end in December 2009, we would view any rallies in dry freight rates that occur before September as based on shaky foundations.  This reflects the fact that since 1949 the US ISM has tended to hit rock bottom four months before a US recession ends.  Adopting a bullish view on dry freight today would be taking a view that the US economy will move out of recession by July, which we view as a low probability event. 

Moreover dry freight rates also ha

ve to contend with adverse supply side fundamentals. Indeed despite a pick up in cancellations and expected slippages in delivery, we expect this will not be sufficient to offset new build deliveries. Our shipping research team expect supply growth of 1.6% in 2009 and 8.7% in 2010, which we believe will sustain strong headwinds for dry freight rates into next year. We believe the main risk to this trade would be a more vigorous upturn in global growth and specifically Asain export growth. ###### **Figure 3: Asian export growth & the US ISM** 65 ISM (3MMA, lagged 6 month) (lhs) 40

Unlike other reflation trades which have been performing relatively strongly over the past few weeks, the nickel to gold price ratio has remained close to its all time lows hit during February. While the ratio may be being distorted by gold ETF buying, we believe new lows in the nickel to gold price ratio are inconsistent with the strong performance in many reflationary trades over the past few weeks. This annual survey is one of the most keenly watched reports as it provides the first glimpse of future acreage a

nd hence production for the major US crops, such as corn, soybeans, wheat and cotton. We find that since 1999 corn prices have displayed the greatest sensitivity to this report with prices rising (falling) when US farmers declare their intention to cut (increase) corn plantings. We believe this reflects the fact that the US represents approximately 60% of world corn exports and consequently changes in US acreage levels can have an important bearing on global export markets. Aside from an outright long in the May’09 corn future, another route to express a bullish corn price view would be to position for the corn forward curve to flatten, that is going long May’09 vs. short Dec’09 corn. However, we would caution that even if US farmers declare their intention to cut corn acreage, historically the positive effect on price has tended to fade. This may reflect the fact that between the US Prospective Plantings survey at the end of March and the more reliable Acreage report at the end of June US farmers have tended to increase their corn plantings from their initial projection made at the end of March. The DB Commodity Harvest index operates by taking a short position in the S&PGSCI Light Energy Index and taking a long position in the same index. However, instead of rolling the futures contracts on a pre-defined scheduled (typically monthly) we apply the Optimum Yield (OY) technology to the 21 of the 24 components of the S&PGSCI Light Energy Index. When commodity forward curves are in backwardation the long and short legs will most often be rolling into the same contract. However, contango allows the OY technology to extract carry or the risk premium via its ability to roll further along the curve. We bel

ieve the main hazard to the performance of the DB Commodity Harvest Index is when a commodity forward curve moves from contango to backwardation.  When this occurs, the strategy to go long the back end of the commodity forward curve and short the front end leg will suddenly trigger a drawdown event.  At the moment 18 of the 21 commodities that employ the OY technology in the DB Commodity Harvest Index have forward curves in contango.  Consequently, the long position of most commodities is set somewhere between the front month contract and the 12-month futures contract, with the average maturity being five months.  A sudden flattening of all commodity forward curves, caused for instance by a rally in spot prices, which is not reflected in the forward curve would lead to a drawdown event. 

In the scenario of a complete flattening of all 18 commodity forward curves, that is for each commodity spot prices move such that they are equal to the futures contract on which the index is long, the Harvest index would suffer a drawdown of 3.20% as of March 27, 2009. Most of these losses (1.70%) originate in the energy

While we have outlined the risks above, we believe the downturn in global growth will sustain commodity forward curves in contango.  Indeed contango is the normal term structure for commodity curves in recessionary environments because the collapse in demand and the subsequent rise in inventories not only tends to dampen volatility in that commodity, but, it also reduces the convenience yield, that is the benefit that accrues to an owner of a physical commodity.  As a result, forward curves ultimately become a function of interest rate and storage costs over time. 

However, we believe investors need to be alert to curve flattening and the risk of backwardation appearing in the event of an unforeseen supply disruption.  In the agricultural sector this could be triggered by droughts. Gold possess some unusual characteristics not found in other commodity markets.  In our view, one of the most obvious is that annual mine production represents just 1.5% of above ground inventories.  However, for most industrial metals, annual mine production is equivalent to 10 times of annual inventory. Consequently, disruptions to supply tend to have less of an effect on the gold market than they would if they occurred in the industrial metals complex. 

We believe inventories and specifically inventory-toconsumption ratios are the ultimate drivers of a commodity price, its forward curve and the level of implied volatility.  This reflects the importance of the Theory of Storage and the existence of convenience yield such that the forward curve and the spot price are defined as: 

Forward price = Spot price + interest rate – (convenience yield – storage costs) 

This formula relies on the fact that by storing rather than selling the commodity, one surrenders the spot price but incurs interest rate and warehousing costs.  However, offsetting these costs, are the benefits accruing from holding inventory, or what is called the convenience yield. A holder of inventories in a particular commodity generates a convenience yield.  This is the flow of services and benefits that accrues to an owner of a physical commodity, but, not to an owner of a contract for future delivery of that same commodity.  This can come in the form of having a secure supply of raw materials and hence eliminating the costs associated with stock-outs. 

Not surprisingly convenience yields trend higher for those commodity markets which have low and declining levels of inventories.  Put another way, the convenience yield rises as the market’s precariousness increases.  This makes intuitive sense since in tightening market conditions consumers attach a greater benefit to the physical ownership of a commodity.  In the current environment of weakening demand and rising inventories for crude oil and industrial metals, this will tend to lower the convenience yield and forward curves become a function largely of interest rate and warehousing costs. 

However, in gold the surge in investment via physically backed gold ETFs is, in our view, leading to increasing concerns of the physical availability of gold.  As a result, it is encouraging the convenience yield to rise and the gold forward curve to flatten.  In the event of financial market panic and more significant flows into physically backed gold ETFs the gold forward would most probably move into backwardation.  Since October last year, the SPRD gold ETF has increased its gold holdings by over 400 tonnes to more than 1,000 tonnes, Figure 1.  As a result, we believe positioning for backwardation in the gold forward curve would be taking a view on deflation and extreme financial market dislocation.

###### **Obama’s 2010 budget proposal recommendation** 

According to the President’s 2010 budget document submitted to the Congress, “the administration is developing a comprehensive energy and climate change plan to invest in clean energy, [and] end our addiction to oil, address the global climate crisis.”  After enactment of the budget, Obama pledged to work expeditiously with key stakeholders and the Congress to develop an economy-wide emissions reduction program to reduce greenhouse gas emissions approximately 14% below 2005 levels by 2020, and approximately 83% below 2005 levels by 2050. 

The Obama administration has proposed that the program be implemented through a cap-and-trade system, saying that this policy approach dramatically reduced acid rain at much lower costs than the trad

itional government regulations and mandates of the past.  Although there have been stories that Obama might be flexible on the issue, so far, the White House is sticking to the concept of a 100% auction of carbon allowances “to ensure that the biggest polluters do not enjoy windfall profits.” Auction revenues are estimated to amount to some USD80 billion per year starting in 2012. 

The budget document also says that the program “will fund vital investments in a clean energy future totaling USD150 billion over 10 years, starting in FY 2012,” and that “the balance [circa USD65 billion/year] of the auction revenues will be returned to the people.” 

###### **Congressional activity** 

There has been little movement in the US Senate.  In early January, Sen. ### **Glossary** 

**API#2** – TFS API#2 ® average price index for coal delivered CIF ARA.  A **PI#4** – TFS API#4 ® average price index for coal loading FOB Richards Bay, South Africa. 

**ARA** : Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp – major delivery hub for cargo entering Northwest Europe. 

**ATS:** Aviation Trading Scheme – this is a carbon-trading scheme for the aviation sector in the EU, and will run parallel to the broader EU-ETS from 2012. All flights entering and leaving the EU will be covered by the ATS from this date. 

**Bcf** : Billion cubic feet – macro measure of natural gas volume. 

**Bunkers:** Fuel oil used to power ships. 

**CAT** : Cumulative average temperature. The sum of daily high + low)/2, usually over a month or season. 

**CDD** : Cooling degree day – excess of daily average temperature over 65°F; usually cumulated over time. 

**CDM** : Clean Development Mechanism – one of the Kyoto Protocol’s two “flexible mechanisms” that allows carbon offsets known as CERs (Certified Emissions Reductions) to be produced. CERs can then be used in the EU-ETS for compliance purposes.
